answer.exemplar: On the globe every parallel is a circle whose circumference falls as the cosine of its latitude, so the 60 degree parallel is half the length of the equator. A cylindrical sheet cannot shrink with latitude, so it draws every parallel at the equator's length, which stretches the high-latitude one by the reciprocal of that cosine. The stretch is a linear one along the parallel, and area responds to the square of a linear stretch, so the fourfold figure on such a sheet is the square of the twofold distortion in one direction. Because the north-south direction is left almost untouched, the excess appears as an east-west stretch, which is why Greenland and the Canadian north look broad and flat while their true outlines are narrow and tall.

questions.explanation: The inflation is a consequence of holding one dimension fixed while the other is stretched. Every parallel on a globe is shorter than the equator by the cosine of its latitude, and the sheet cannot shorten them, so the sheet draws a length of ground at the 60 degree parallel as though it lay along the equator, stretching it twofold, and area follows the square of any linear stretch, which gives the fourfold area figure. The equator is the case where the cosine is one and nothing is stretched, so the error there is zero, and that is why the growth with latitude is smooth rather than sudden. The trap is to attribute the effect to a mistake in the drawing: it is a structural consequence of flattening a sphere, and the same mechanism produces the familiar poleward crowding of the whole sheet.
questions.hint: Compare the length of a parallel on the globe with its length on the sheet.

answer.exemplar: A grid records one number per cell, so the resolution sets both the storage and the processing cost, and moving from 30 metres to 2 metres multiplies the number of cells by more than two hundred, which is a budget decision before it is a mapping one. Resolution also sets what can be seen: a 30 metre cell averages a terrace lip into the slope behind it, and no amount of processing recovers a feature the cell never measured. Finer is therefore better only where the feature being mapped is larger than the cell, and worse in two other ways, since the instrument noise of the source is spread over a smaller area and any error in it is harder to average out. The defensible choice is to keep the coarse model for the district and add the fine one only for the terrace.

questions.explanation: Resolution buys detail at a price paid in three places at once. The cost scales with the number of cells, so the fine grid is roughly two hundred and twenty-five times larger than the coarse one, and processing and delivery costs follow. The second cost is interpretive: a 30 metre cell is an average over the whole cell, and a terrace lip narrower than the cell is not there to be found, so no algorithm recovers it from a number that already lost it. The third is instrumental, because a sensor's error is being recorded over a smaller patch and is therefore harder to see as noise. The point of the case is that the two grids answer different questions, and asking for the fine one does not make the coarse model wrong so much as irrelevant to the terrace.
questions.hint: Separate the cost of storing the extra cells from the fact that the extra detail may not exist.
questions.learningObjective: explain the trade-off behind the resolution of an elevation model

A one-metre claim therefore refers to where a line was plotted, not to what the line represents on the ground, and a line plotted to a metre can still enclose a field that is fifty metres across. The two statements are not in contradiction so much as answering different questions, and the catalogue entry uses one number to cover both, which is how the confusion arises. questions.explanation: The two figures answer different questions and a catalogue entry has collapsed them into one. A one-metre accuracy is then a statement about where the pen was placed relative to other pen placements, which is a real and checkable claim, and it is not a claim about what the drawn shape represents. answer.exemplar: The join is between a count of households and a denominator of people, and nothing in the operation converts one into the other, so the two figures cannot be divided. Household size differs between places, so a catchment of 4,000 households may be 9,000 people in one district and 11,000 in another, and dollars per head divided by households is not a meaningful rate at all. The result is a column that looks like a sales density and is not one, and the error is invisible in the output because the join succeeded. The remedy is to convert both to a common unit, usually people, before joining, and to state that conversion; the source grid usually provides it. The general point is that a spatial join transfers values between locations while leaving their units untouched, so the analyst rather than the software is responsible for whether the arithmetic is meaningful.

questions.explanation: A spatial join matches locations and copies attributes across, and it does nothing at all to the units of the attributes it copies, so a mismatch survives the operation intact and looks no different afterwards. Here one side counts households and the other divides money by people, and a household is not a person: the ratio between them varies from district to district with household size, so the same 4,000 figure denotes a different number of customers in each place and the resulting column has no unit that can be named. This is the general hazard in joining layers assembled for different purposes, and it is worst where the layers are both plausible and both numeric, since a wrong rate still sorts and still averages. The fix is to state a common unit before joining, which means obtaining a household-size figure rather than assuming one, and to record that assumption alongside the output.

The standard remedy is to dissolve the union of the layers before totalling, so each piece of ground contributes once, and to keep a separate count of the areas affected by each layer separately. answer.exemplar: The impedance is what the analysis minimises, so equal cost per kilometre makes it minimise distance. A catchment drawn that way is the set of places from which the hospital is nearest in kilometres, which ignores that the congested road a short distance away is slower to travel than the longer road that is clear. In a network where traffic is heavy on the routes closest to a city centre, that difference is not a detail: the distance-based catchment will reach into districts whose real journey time puts them outside the service area, and will shrink away from districts on a bypass that is longer but faster. The fix is to use travel time or a generalised cost as the impedance, which needs a network built from observed speeds rather than a straight-line distance. The result is that the same catchment can move substantially once the impedance is changed, and it is the impedance, not the data, that the planner has chosen.

questions.explanation: The impedance is the quantity the analysis makes as small as possible, and choosing a flat cost per kilometre therefore makes it a distance search rather than a time search. What that produces is a set of places that are close in kilometres, which is not the same set as the places from which the journey is quickest, and the two diverge wherever traffic is uneven, which is everywhere in a network that funnels into a town. The consequence for a hospital catchment is direct: a densely built district on congested roads can fall outside the service area while a sparser one further out along a bypass falls inside it, and the map is then being used to justify a siting decision it cannot support. Choosing travel time as the impedance, and building the network from observed speeds rather than from straight lines, is what makes the catchment a statement about access rather than about geometry.

answer.exemplar: Two requirements pull in opposite directions. A shop or a clinic needs enough customers to cover its costs, which sets a minimum population for the function and therefore a minimum size for the settlement that supports it. At the same time, the supplier needs to reach enough customers before anyone can supply the next settlement up, which sets a maximum range, and a customer wants the service nearer than that range allows. The two constraints meet at a spacing that is therefore fairly regular, and a settlement of twice or two and a half times the size of the next one down can support the higher-order function with a longer range. Real hierarchies are less tidy than this because transport costs, relief, and the presence of a second centre all perturb the pattern, which is why the figures come out as a range rather than as an exact ratio.

questions.explanation: The regularity is the product of a floor and a ceiling that happen to be compatible. A business needs a minimum turnover to cover its costs, so a settlement below a certain population cannot support a particular function and it travels to the next settlement up, which puts a floor under the size of any centre offering it. The supplier faces the mirror-image constraint, since a shop that stocks a more demanding range of goods needs more customers than is available in one small place and so extends its range, which puts a ceiling on the spacing between centres of the same order. Where the two constraints agree, the spacing is regular and each level is a roughly constant multiple of the one below, which is what the ratio in the question records. The imperfections are equally real, since relief, poor roads and a competing centre all stretch or compress the pattern, and the ratio changes with the function being measured.

questions.explanation: A superstore is a higher-order function: it supplies a range and a spending habit that a small shop cannot match, and by locating itself where land is cheap it captures the demand that used to be spent in the centre. What remains at the centre is the low-order function, and a small shop's threshold is a share of the population's spending, so when the higher-order trade moves out the centre may fall below the level at which one shop can trade. The opening two streets further out is the counter-movement in the same process, since a developer will put a small shop where the remaining footfall now concentrates. The pattern is a reordering of the hierarchy under retail change rather than a change in the population, which is what the options that blame headcount get wrong.

questions.explanation: The first requirement is the data itself, since without a value in each band there is nothing to classify, and the second is the labelled sample, since a supervised method cannot assign a class it has not been shown. Only after both does the rule get derived and applied across the whole image, and only after that is there anything to test, which is why the validation step comes last. The test has to be on pixels held back from the rule rather than on the pixels that built it, since a rule evaluated on its own training data will appear to be perfect. The ordering that puts the check earlier has nothing to check, and the one that derives the rule before reading the bands has nothing to derive it from.
questions.hint: Each operation needs something the previous one produced, so the order is forced by dependency.
